title: The Ground Under the Cities: a Farmer's Apprenticeship, the Slave South, and the Invention of a Profession
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Hartford, the eighth generation on the river
stops.date_confidence: attested; birth date and parentage given by Wikipedia and the National Park Service biography
stops.campa: John Olmsted keeps a dry-goods store on Main Street, eighth generation of his family on this bend of the Connecticut, and on the twenty-sixth of April his wife Charlotte Law Hull Olmsted bears him a son. The trade is steady, the household comfortable, the town small enough that a merchant's boy is known by name in it. Charlotte dies before he is four, of an overdose of medicine the family record never fully explains. For most of the next fifteen years the boy is boarded out to country ministers in other towns, a year or two at a time.
suggested_refs: The Olmsted family's Hartford dry-goods trade, eight generations on the Connecticut River
sources: National Park Service, Frederick Law Olmsted National Historic Site biography

stops.name: North Guilford, boarded with the gardening minister
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: c. 1829, month and day unknown and defaulted; the placement comes from Roper's biography by way of the dossier, not from a fetched primary source; village-center coordinate, the house not identified
stops.campa: At about seven he is sent down to the Reverend Zolva Whitmore at North Guilford, a minister who gardens. His mother is three years dead and his father has remarried Mary Ann Bull; the Hartford house has a new mistress. In old age Olmsted will name North Guilford the one idyll of the boarding-out years, and what he remembers of it is ground: a woodlot, a farm, a village street where men talk soil and weather, and whole afternoons to walk in all of it with nobody waiting to test him at the end of the day.
suggested_refs: The parsonage and glebe of the Reverend Zolva Whitmore at North Guilford
sources: Laura Wood Roper, FLO: A Biography of Frederick Law Olmsted (1973), as relayed by the dossier

stops.name: Newington, five years under Joab Brace
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: c. 1832-1837, month and day unknown and defaulted; Roper by way of the dossier
stops.campa: The Reverend Joab Brace of Newington takes him for what becomes the longest single placement of his boyhood, close to five years of scripture, recitation, and field labor on a strict clock. Olmsted remembers it without affection: severity from the master, bullying from the other boys, and a child who would rather be out in the lots looking at things held to his books instead. He is being educated, in the only sense the arrangement intends. Nothing on the schedule is landscape. The placement runs until 1837, when his father takes him out of it and sends him to Andover.
suggested_refs: The Reverend Joab Brace's household at Newington, longest of the boarding placements
sources: Laura Wood Roper, FLO: A Biography of Frederick Law Olmsted (1973), as relayed by the dossier

stops.name: Andover, surveying with Frederick Barton
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1837, month and day unknown and defaulted; the dossier's geography lens gave 1838-1839 and the verifier ruled against it on the Wikipedia text, which has him beginning in 1837 and leaving when Barton left in 1838
stops.campa: He is sent to Phillips Academy at Andover in 1837 to study surveying and topographical engineering with Frederick Augustus Barton, and for a year the schooling finally fits the boy. It is the only technical training he ever receives: he lays out the ground under Central Park, the Capitol, and a world's fair without a degree in engineering or in anything else. What Andover gives him is a chain and a compass, hypothetical towns drawn out on paper, rocks and plants collected on the walk back. When Barton leaves the academy in 1838, Olmsted leaves with him.
suggested_refs: Phillips Academy, Andover, and Frederick Augustus Barton's surveying instruction, 1837-1838

stops.name: New Haven, the eyes and the degree not taken
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: standard biography (Roper 1973; Rybczynski 1999) places him at New Haven in 1842 as a non-matriculated auditor, month and day unknown and defaulted. The dossier's flat claim that he was never a Yale student is overstated and its 1837 New Haven dating unsupported; Wikipedia gives the sumac poisoning no year and no place. Yale's own archival page could not be fetched
stops.campa: Sumac poisoning has weakened his eyes badly enough that a physician tells him to give up any thought of a degree. He comes to New Haven anyway, in 1842, to be near his brother John Hull, and sits in on lectures as a young man with no matriculation and no examinations ahead of him. The popular story that he attended Yale and the flat denial that he was ever there are both wrong. Yale's register does not carry him, because he never entered it in the sense the register means, and Yale's own archival account of the arrangement could not be consulted.
suggested_refs: Yale College lecture attendance by non-matriculated auditors in the 1840s
sources: Wikipedia, 'Frederick Law Olmsted' (sumac poisoning, abandoned college plans)
Roper (1973) and Rybczynski, A Clearing in the Distance (1999), as relayed by the dossier

stops.name: Beaver Street, the French silk house
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the dossier gives 1840-1842 and cites Wikipedia, but the verifier found the article does not carry the Benkard and Hutton detail; month and day unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: For roughly eighteen months he clerks at the Beaver Street counting house of James Benkard and Benjamin Hutton, importers of French silks, in the dense commercial blocks at the foot of Manhattan. He is nineteen, and at home the post is understood as an answer to the long question of what is to be done with Frederick. It is not. A young man can spend every working hour inside a great city and see nothing of the city, and what he sees of this one is ledgers, invoices, and bales carried past a doorway.
suggested_refs: The Beaver Street silk-importing house of Benkard and Hutton
sources: Laura Wood Roper, FLO (1973), as relayed by the dossier
Dossier geography lens, source attribution corrected by the verify stage

stops.name: South Street, the Ronaldson sails for Canton
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the sailing date, the ship, and Captain Warren Fox come from Roper by way of the dossier; the verifier confirmed that the Wikipedia article the dossier cited carries none of it
stops.campa: Two days short of his twenty-first birthday he signs as an apprentice seaman aboard the bark Ronaldson, Captain Warren Fox, bound for Canton by way of the Cape of Good Hope. He has never been to sea. The voyage will run a year, through scurvy, brutal labor, and a crew close to mutiny, and it teaches him what no farm and no counting house could have: what a badly run confined community does to the people shut inside it. For now there is only the bark working down the harbor past the shipping of South Street, and Olmsted forward on her with the crew.
suggested_refs: The bark Ronaldson, New York to Canton, 1843-1844
sources: Laura Wood Roper, FLO (1973), as relayed by the dossier

stops.name: Whampoa, the anchorage below Canton
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: September 1843, day unknown and defaulted; coordinate approximate to the modern Huangpu district
stops.campa: The Ronaldson comes up to the Whampoa anchorage below Canton, where the foreign ships lie at their moorings and the tea, cassia, and raw silk come down to them by lighter. Olmsted is sick through much of it and ashore very little, a sailor among sailors at the edge of an empire he sees mostly as cargo passing over a rail. A year of his life goes into the passage out and the passage home, and the great voyage of his youth gives him almost no China at all.
suggested_refs: The Whampoa anchorage and the Canton tea and silk trade of the 1840s
sources: Laura Wood Roper, FLO (1973), as relayed by the dossier

stops.name: Cheshire, learning the ground from his uncle
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the dossier gives 1844-1845 at Cheshire and 1846-1847 at Geddes's farm; month and day unknown and defaulted to the summer after the Ronaldson's return of 15 April 1844
stops.campa: The Ronaldson lands him back in New York in April 1844, and by summer he is at Cheshire studying scientific agriculture with his uncle David Brooks, then on to George Geddes's noted farm near Syracuse. Drainage, rotation, soils, grafting, the arithmetic of yield: he takes it seriously and reads everything on it that is in print. This is the habit he keeps for life, learning an entire technical field from the ground up with nobody certifying that he has. It is the third or fourth attempt to find him a vocation, and the first that holds.
suggested_refs: George Geddes's farm at Fairmount near Syracuse, a model of improved practice
sources: Laura Wood Roper, FLO (1973), as relayed by the dossier

stops.name: Tosomock Farm, the pears and the curving drive
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia gives the 125-acre farm and January 1848; coordinate corrected to the surviving Olmsted-Beil House at 4515 Hylan Boulevard, the dossier's pin having landed 5 km north in mid-island
stops.campa: In January his father buys him one hundred and twenty-five acres on the south shore of Staten Island, and here Olmsted farms for seven years. He curves the entrance drive instead of running it straight, moves the outbuildings clear of the view, deepens a pond, sets orchards, and takes a prize for his pears; seven years of arranging a piece of ground, and he cannot leave off doing it. His father had earlier bought him a shore farm at Sachem's Head in Guilford, too rocky to pay. This one does not reliably pay either. He holds it until 1855.
suggested_refs: The Olmsted-Beil House, 4515 Hylan Boulevard, Staten Island, surviving farmhouse of Tosomock Farm

segments.name: The Traveling Writer: England and the Slave South

stops.name: Liverpool, ashore with his brother and Brace
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day unknown, defaulted to the start of the six-month walking tour
stops.campa: He lands at Liverpool with his brother John Hull and their friend Charles Loring Brace, three young Americans with knapsacks and six months to walk in England and on the Continent. He is twenty-eight, a Staten Island market gardener with no profession, and the thing that will decide the rest of his life is sitting four miles across the Mersey. The city is coal smoke, dock traffic, and blackened stone, and what Olmsted the farmer notices first is what the air is doing to the surfaces of things.
stops.quote: every thing out of doors here soon gets toned down
stops.quote_source: Frederick Law Olmsted, Walks and Talks of an American Farmer in England, Part 1 (Project Gutenberg #77164), on Liverpool's coal smoke
suggested_refs: Walks and Talks of an American Farmer in England (1852), the book made from this tour
sources: Olmsted, Walks and Talks of an American Farmer in England (Project Gutenberg #77164)

stops.name: Birkenhead Park, the People's Garden
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1850; the day is arbitrary, set only to place the visit inside the tour. Coordinate corrected to the park itself, both dossier lenses having pinned Birkenhead town centre, 1.8 km and 2.2 km off in different directions
stops.campa: A baker at Birkenhead tells them they must not leave without seeing the park, so they walk out to it: land laid out from Joseph Paxton's plan and opened in 1847, with winding walks, water, and meadow, and the through traffic carried around the outside. What stops Olmsted is not the planting. It is that the ground belongs to the people of the town and that a working man's family walks it on the same footing as anyone else. He calls it a People's Garden and writes that democratic America has nothing to be thought of as comparable with it.
suggested_refs: Birkenhead Park, opened 5 April 1847 from Joseph Paxton's plan, the first publicly funded park in Britain

stops.name: New York, the farmer's book and the Times commission
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year 1852 for both the book and the commission; month and day unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: Walks and Talks of an American Farmer in England comes out in 1852 and makes him, at thirty, a writer. Henry J. Raymond of the New-York Daily Times reads him and offers a commission: go south, travel among the slave states, and report what the system actually does to land, to labor, and to the people living by it. Olmsted takes it the way a farmer takes a survey rather than the way an abolitionist takes a cause. Three years on the road will come out of it, and three books, and at last the wartime abridgment called The Cotton Kingdom.
suggested_refs: The New-York Daily Times Southern letters, signed Yeoman, 1853-1854

stops.name: Richmond, the arithmetic of a slave's labor
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the dossier gives 1853-1854 for the Virginia leg and cites Wikipedia, which the verifier found does not carry it; month and day set to place the leg in order
stops.campa: He works Virginia first, the upland farms, the tobacco country, the slave-hiring market of Richmond, and he keeps the books he was trained to keep. He counts the hands in a field and the acres they cover, prices the hire of a man for a year, asks after fencing and manure and the state of the plows. The question he puts is not whether slavery is wicked but what it costs, per acre, per task, per day, measured against free labor in the states across the line. He finds it dear, wasteful, and self-perpetuating, and he says so in columns of figures rather than in appeals. The letters go north to the Times over the signature Yeoman.
stops.quote: The cash value of a slave's labour in Virginia is, practically, the cash value of the same labour minus the cost of its transportation, acclimatizing, and breaking in to cotton-culture in Mississippi.
stops.quote_source: Frederick Law Olmsted, The Cotton Kingdom, vol. 1, ch. I (Project Gutenberg #72676)
suggested_refs: A Journey in the Seaboard Slave States (1856)

stops.name: New Orleans, where his brother turns back
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the dossier gives 1853-1854 and a Wikipedia attribution the verifier could not confirm; month and day unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: The brothers come down to New Orleans together and there John Hull's tuberculosis ends his part in the journey. He turns back; Frederick goes on into the Deep South alone. Olmsted has a traveler's manners and a reporter's patience, and he sits at plantation tables while men explain their own accounts to him. What he writes about the field hands he watches carries the racial contempt of his time openly, in the same sentence that calls them brethren.
stops.quote: But the great mass, as they are seen at work, under overseers, in the fields, appear very dull, idiotic, and brute-like; and it requires an effort to appreciate that they are, very much more than the beasts they drive, our brethren—a part of ourselves.
stops.quote_source: Frederick Law Olmsted, The Cotton Kingdom, vol. 1, ch. III (Project Gutenberg #72676)
suggested_refs: A Journey in the Back Country (1860)
sources: Dossier geography lens, source attribution corrected by the verify stage

stops.name: San Antonio, money for the German paper
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1854 for the Texas leg, with the Zeitung support tied by the dossier to 1857 as well; month and day set to order the route
stops.campa: In San Antonio he finds the free-soil German colonists of the hill country and the exile Adolf Douai, whose San Antonio Zeitung prints against slavery inside a slave state and is being strangled for it. Olmsted quietly raises money to keep the paper alive. A Journey through Texas comes out of this leg, part of it built from his brother's notes taken before the illness sent him home. From Eagle Pass he rides across the Rio Grande and back, and the exact ford is not recorded.
stops.quote: and the citizens of the cotton States, as a whole, are poor. They work little, and that little, badly; they earn little, they sell little; they buy little, and they have little—very little—of the common comforts and consolations of civilized life.
stops.quote_source: Frederick Law Olmsted, The Cotton Kingdom, vol. 1, ch. I (Project Gutenberg #72676)
suggested_refs: Adolf Douai's San Antonio Zeitung and the Texas free-soil German settlements
A Journey through Texas (1857)
sources: Dossier cross-reference to standard biography, consistent with Eric Foner, Free Soil, Free Labor, Free Men

stops.name: Central Park, superintendent under the chief engineer
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the 1857 appointment is from the dossier crawl and was not re-fetched from a primary New York parks source; month and day set to order the segment
stops.campa: The park commission hires him in 1857 as superintendent of the works, under chief engineer Egbert Viele, on the recommendation of men who know him as an author with a failed publishing house behind him: Dix and Edwards has just gone down in the Panic. It is patronage work, and he takes it because he needs the salary; nobody has yet asked him what the park ought to look like. The job is gangs of laborers clearing rock and swamp above Fifty-ninth Street, in a district of shanties, bone-boiling yards, and loose pigs, with the built city still a long way south of it.
stops.quote: Only twenty years ago, Union Square was "out of town;" twenty years hence, the town will have enclosed the Central Park.
stops.quote_source: Olmsted and Vaux, Description of a Plan for the Improvement of the Central Park (1858; Project Gutenberg #73830)
suggested_refs: Egbert Viele's 1856 topographical survey of the Central Park site
sources: Dossier chronology lens, tagged R and not independently re-fetched
Olmsted and Vaux, Description of a Plan (Project Gutenberg #73830)

stops.name: Seneca Village, the ground already emptied
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1857 for the final evictions, before Olmsted became architect-in-chief; day unknown and defaulted. The dossier's afterlife lens pins the site 400 m from its geography lens; the geography value is used and the disagreement is unresolved
stops.campa: Between West Eighty-second and Eighty-ninth Streets stands Seneca Village: some two hundred and twenty-five people, roughly two thirds of them Black, with three churches, a school, and enough property among the men to carry the vote. The city has taken the land by eminent domain and the last residents are put out in October 1857, before Olmsted is made architect-in-chief. He did not order the taking. The ground reaches him already emptied, and nothing he writes afterward mentions what stood on it.
suggested_refs: Sara Cedar Miller, Before Central Park (2022)
Central Park Conservancy archaeology and interpretation at the Seneca Village site
sources: Central Park Conservancy, Seneca Village history
Rosenzweig and Blackmar, The Park and the People (1992)

stops.name: The Mall, the plan that beat thirty-two others
stops.date_confidence: attested to April 1858 for the competition result and May 1858 for the appointment as architect-in-chief; day unknown and defaulted. The $2,500 salary figure is [R], not re-verified
stops.campa: In April the commissioners judge thirty-three entries and award the prize to number thirty-three, the Greensward plan of Olmsted and the architect Calvert Vaux, who had proposed the partnership to him. The plan sinks four transverse roads below grade so the city's cross-town traffic passes under the park without ever entering it, and hands the whole surface to people on foot. In May he is made architect-in-chief at twenty-five hundred dollars a year, with Vaux as consulting architect.
stops.quote: They must be constantly open to all the legitimate traffic of the city, to coal carts and butchers' carts, dust carts and dung carts;
stops.quote_source: Olmsted and Vaux, Description of a Plan for the Improvement of the Central Park (1858; Project Gutenberg #73830), on the four transverse roads; the sentence continues in the source
suggested_refs: The Greensward plan drawings, entry number 33 in the 1858 Central Park competition
Robert Smithson, 'Frederick Law Olmsted and the Dialectical Landscape,' Artforum, February 1973
sources: Olmsted and Vaux, Description of a Plan (Project Gutenberg #73830)

stops.name: New York, marrying his brother's widow
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia gives 13 June 1859 and names Mayor Daniel Fawcett Tiemann as officiant. John Hull Olmsted's own death date and place are not in the verified pool and are not asserted here
stops.campa: John Hull Olmsted, his companion on the English walk and on the road to New Orleans, is dead of the tuberculosis that turned him back at the city. On the thirteenth of June, Frederick marries his brother's widow, Mary Cleveland Perkins Olmsted, and takes her three children as his own; the mayor of New York, Daniel Fawcett Tiemann, performs the ceremony. They will have children of their own and bury more than one of them. He is thirty-seven, and running the largest public works in America.
suggested_refs: Mary Cleveland Perkins Olmsted and the household of the Central Park years

stops.name: Paris, an evening with Alphand
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the dossier gives 1859 for the leave of absence and the meetings with Alphand and Sir Richard Mayne, without month; day and month set to order the segment after the June marriage. Canonical Paris pin inherited unchanged
stops.campa: On leave from the park he crosses to study how Europe administers public ground. In Paris he calls on Jean-Charles-Adolphe Alphand, the engineer running Haussmann's parks, promenades, and plantations, and they go over nursery practice, drainage, road section, and the cost of keeping a city's trees alive year on year. No American park has yet been obliged to ask any of it. In London he puts a different question to the police commissioner Sir Richard Mayne: how is a crowd inside a public park actually policed?
suggested_refs: Alphand's Service des promenades et plantations under Haussmann
Alphand, Les Promenades de Paris (1867-1873)
sources: Dossier chronology lens, tagged R and not independently re-fetched

segments.name: System Has Ruled: the Sanitary Commission

stops.name: Washington, general secretary of the Sanitary Commission
stops.date_confidence: attested: the commission was created 18 June 1861 and the dossier gives 20 June for Olmsted's appointment as general secretary
stops.campa: Henry Whitney Bellows brings him to Washington as general secretary of the United States Sanitary Commission, authorized that June with Abraham Lincoln's approval, and Olmsted takes leave from the park to run it. The commission is a civilian body with no command authority, charged with the health of an army that has almost no medical organization of its own: camp inspection, diet, latrines, water supply, nurses, stores. He builds it the way he builds everything, on paper first and from the top down. His appointment is dated 20 June, two days after the commission itself exists.
suggested_refs: The United States Sanitary Commission, authorized 18 June 1861

stops.name: White House Landing, the hospital transports
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1862 for the Peninsula Campaign hospital-transport work; month and day set to the campaign's advance up the York. The dossier misspelled the commanding general as McLellan; he is George B. McClellan
stops.campa: On the Virginia Peninsula, with McClellan's army pushing toward Richmond, Olmsted takes charge of evacuating the wounded and turns river steamers into hospital transports on the York and the James. The commission can order nothing and command nobody, so what happens here happens because he has arranged it in advance. Katharine Prescott Wormeley, who is there, sets down what the order he imposes is worth in such a place. He works the decks himself, among surgeons, volunteer women, and men carried aboard by the hundred out of the mud.
stops.quote: Happily system has ruled in the work of the Sanitary Commission, and such success as has attended its operations is chiefly due to this
stops.quote_source: Hospital Transports (1863; Project Gutenberg #52122), in the connective narrative between the compiled letters. Gutenberg credits Olmsted as author; the 1863 title page names no author, only 'Compiled and Published at the request of the Sanitary Commission'
suggested_refs: Hospital Transports (1863), compiled at the request of the Sanitary Commission
Katharine Prescott Wormeley, The Other Side of War (1889)

stops.name: Vicksburg, the western branches he cannot govern
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the dossier gives 1863 for the western tour by Cincinnati, Chicago, and St. Louis to Grant's encampment, without month; month and day set to order the segment
stops.campa: He goes west by Cincinnati, Chicago, and St. Louis to Grant's lines at Vicksburg, inspecting the commission's western branches, which raise their own money, run their own depots, and have no wish to be administered from Washington. The business here is stores moving from the northern towns down to the siege lines, and the men who move them answer to their own committees. Olmsted wants one national organization under one head, audited, uniform, answerable. The branches want their own towns' supplies to reach their own towns' boys. He loses the argument.
suggested_refs: The semi-autonomous western branches of the Sanitary Commission at Chicago and St. Louis
sources: Dossier residences-and-migrations table, consistent with USSC administrative history; source attribution corrected by the verify stage

stops.name: Washington, the resignation
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the dossier gives 1 September 1863 for the resignation and the decision to go to California. The dossier's Gettysburg relief claim was struck by the verifier as unattested and carries no stop in this file
stops.campa: The executive committee refuses him the centralized national control he has been demanding, and he resigns. George Templeton Strong, who sits on that committee and admires him, had already written the diagnosis into his diary in March: talent and energy most rare, absolute purity and disinterestedness, and a monomania for organization on paper. Olmsted is forty-one, out of the park, out of the commission, and in debt. A California mining company offers him ten thousand dollars a year to manage an estate he has never seen.
stops.quote: Prominent defects, a monomania for system and organization on paper (elaborate, laboriously thought out, and generally impracticable), and appetite for power. He is a lay-Hildebrand.
stops.quote_source: The Diary of George Templeton Strong, vol. 3, Nevins and Thomas eds., entry of 11 March 1863
suggested_refs: The Diary of George Templeton Strong, vol. 3 (The Civil War, 1860-1865)
sources: Strong diary, vol. 3, verified against the scanned text on archive.org (item gtsvol-3)

stops.name: Panama, crossing the isthmus by rail
stops.date_confidence: attested to September 1863 by the NPS biography; the day is unknown and the month set to order the passage between the Washington resignation and the arrival at Bear Valley
stops.campa: There is no railroad across the continent yet, so California is reached by sea to the Isthmus, by rail across it, and by sea again. Olmsted crosses Panama in a train through country he has no vocabulary for: forest standing in permanent summer, a density of growth that makes New England look thin. Thirty years on he will plant a subtropical border for George Vanderbilt in the Carolina mountains and reach back to this week for it. For now he takes notes on the vegetation as the train runs.
suggested_refs: The Panama Railroad, completed 1855, the crossing used by California-bound travelers before 1869
sources: National Park Service, Frederick Law Olmsted National Historic Site biography

stops.name: Bear Valley, the forty-five thousand acres
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the dossier gives 1863-1865 for the Mariposa management; month and day set to the arrival after the isthmus crossing. Coordinate corrected to Bear Valley, Mariposa County; the dossier's pin lay 12 km east in the Sierra foothills
stops.campa: The Mariposa Estate is some forty-four thousand acres of Sierra foothill with gold under it, and Olmsted arrives at Bear Valley as its manager for a company in New York that has already been sold a story about the ore. He rides the claims, reads the assays, and works out what the company does not want to hear: the values fall off with depth, and the money to sink the shafts properly does not exist. He manages it from Bear Valley for two years. The company fails in 1865.
suggested_refs: Rancho Las Mariposas, 44,387 acres, and the collapse of the Mariposa Company in 1865
sources: Dossier geography lens, source attribution corrected by the verify stage

stops.name: Mountain View Cemetery, the first ground entirely his
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the design commission is dated 1864 by the dossier, though the cemetery itself was established in 1863; the claim that this is his first largely independent executed landscape has no source of its own and is carried as tradition. Month and day unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: Oakland's new rural cemetery was established the year before on a slope looking out over the bay, and its trustees engage him to lay out the ground. It is called the first executed landscape that is his alone, with no Vaux and no commission of politicians over him, though nothing beyond tradition carries that claim. He draws a broad axial avenue up the hill, curving drives held to the contour, dark cypress and pine chosen for a country that goes dry in summer. The execution departs from the drawings in places.
suggested_refs: Mountain View Cemetery, Oakland, established 1863, Olmsted plan 1864
sources: Dossier crawl, tagged R and not independently re-fetched
Wikipedia, 'Mountain View Cemetery (Oakland, California)' for the 1863 establishment

stops.name: Founders' Rock, a college on Strawberry Creek
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the dossier gives 1865 for the College of California plan and 1866 for the unexecuted San Francisco report, which was delivered after he had gone east; month and day set to order the segment
stops.campa: For the College of California he plans a campus at Berkeley with a residential village beside it, streets bent to the falls of the creek, houses set among trees, the whole meant to be a settled place rather than a row of buildings on a lot. In the same season he draws San Francisco a park with a sunken parkway that would double as a firebreak, and that one is never cut. Little of Berkeley is built as drawn either. Piedmont Avenue and the line of Strawberry Creek carry the fragments.
suggested_refs: Olmsted's 1866 Preliminary Report on a park for San Francisco, unexecuted
sources: Dossier geography lens, source attribution corrected by the verify stage

stops.name: Yosemite Valley, the report that was buried
stops.date_confidence: attested to August 1865 for the Preliminary Report; the day is arbitrary. The 1864 Yosemite Grant is attested to that year without a fetched day
stops.campa: Abraham Lincoln signed the valley and the Mariposa Big Tree Grove over to California in 1864, to be held for public use and never sold, and Olmsted sits on the first board of commissioners. He camps in the valley and writes the Preliminary Report: that scenery of this order is a public necessity rather than a luxury, and that government must protect equal access to it against the men who would otherwise own the view and charge at the gate for it. Commissioners with interests of their own keep the report from the legislature. It is not published in full until 1952.
suggested_refs: Olmsted's Yosemite and the Mariposa Grove: A Preliminary Report (1865), unpublished until 1952
Olmsted Point on the Tioga Road, named for Olmsted and his son
sources: National Park Service, Frederick Law Olmsted National Historic Site biography

stops.name: Prospect Park, the one they were let finish
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1865 for the return east and the founding of the firm, and to 1873 for the substantial completion of Prospect Park; month and day unknown and defaulted to the first full year of the Brooklyn work
stops.campa: He resigns Mariposa, comes back east, and he and Vaux take the Brooklyn commission and form Olmsted, Vaux and Company. Prospect Park is the one they get right: no reservoir cut through the middle of it, no gridiron pressing on three sides, a long meadow, a wooded ravine, and water they can run where they please. Design work continues to 1873. Their argument for what a park is for had been written down in New York eight years earlier and had not changed.
stops.quote: the visitor, who, in the best sense is the true owner
stops.quote_source: Olmsted and Vaux, Description of a Plan for the Improvement of the Central Park (1858; Project Gutenberg #73830)
suggested_refs: The Long Meadow and the Ravine, Prospect Park, Brooklyn
sources: Olmsted and Vaux, Description of a Plan (Project Gutenberg #73830)

stops.name: Delaware Park, a whole city strung on parkways
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1868 for the beginning of the Buffalo work; month and day unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: Buffalo asks for a park and Olmsted and Vaux give it three, tied together by planted parkways two hundred feet wide running out through the street grid, so that the whole city sits inside the system instead of beside it. The Park, later Delaware Park, holds the meadow and the lake; the Front looks down the Niagara River; the Parade serves the German east side. It is the first time in America the idea is applied to an entire city at once. Buffalo builds it.
suggested_refs: The Buffalo park and parkway system, from 1868

stops.name: Riverside, streets that follow the river
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1868-1869 for the Riverside design; month and day unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: Nine miles out from Chicago on the Des Plaines, a syndicate wants a suburb, and Olmsted and Vaux lay out streets that curve with the river's own contours, with shared greens, houses set back from the road, and a village center at the railway station. It is the model American developers copy for the next hundred years. The Chicago fire and the crash behind it break the developers' contract, and the designers collect very little of the fee they were promised.
suggested_refs: The village plan of Riverside, Illinois, 1869

stops.name: The Capitol grounds, the marble terrace
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Architect of the Capitol to 1874 for the commission, correcting the dossier's 1873; the dossier's June 1874 presentation of a comprehensive plan to Congress is unattested and is dropped. AOC gives 1875 for the terrace design submission, 1879-1881 for the Summerhouse, and 1882-1892 for the terraces
stops.campa: The partnership with Vaux was dissolved in 1872 for what the two of them called mutual convenience, and Olmsted works alone now. Congress commissions him in 1874 to plan the grounds of the Capitol, and he will spend nearly twenty years on them. He thins the planting so the building can be seen, sets the walks, and builds a small brick summerhouse on the west slope with a spring, a fountain, and shade for people who have climbed the hill in a Washington summer. The marble terrace that gives the west front a base to stand on is fought over for years and is not finished until 1892.
suggested_refs: The Summerhouse on the Capitol's west slope, built 1879-1881
The Olmsted marble terraces of the Capitol, 1882-1892

stops.name: Mount Royal, the mountain read in zones
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the 1874 commission date is plausible but unconfirmed, the Wikipedia article giving only the inauguration of 24 May 1876; month and day set to order the segment. Coordinate corrected to the park, the dossier having pinned downtown Montreal
stops.campa: Montreal gives him a mountain in the middle of the city and he refuses to treat it as a site for effects. He divides it into zones by what already grows there and what each slope will bear, plans a road that climbs by long grades so the view arrives gradually instead of all at once, and tells the city that its real work here is forestry carried on for the next fifty years. The park opens in 1876, partly built. The long forest management does not happen.
suggested_refs: Mount Royal Park, inaugurated 24 May 1876

stops.name: The Back Bay Fens, a sewer made into scenery
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the dossier gives 1878 for the start of the formal Boston work and was not independently re-fetched; month and day unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: Boston's Back Bay Fens is a tidal flat taking the sewage of a growing city, and the commission is a sanitary engineering problem before it is anything else. Olmsted takes it as both: a basin that holds storm water and lets the tide flush it, planted with salt marsh species that will stand brackish water, so that a drainage works reads as a piece of coastline. From here the Muddy River, Jamaica Pond, the Arboretum, and Franklin Park will be strung into one green chain across the city.
stops.quote: The popular idea of the park is a beautiful open space, in which quiet drives, rides, and strolls may be had.
stops.quote_source: Olmsted and Vaux, Description of a Plan for the Improvement of the Central Park (1858; Project Gutenberg #73830)
suggested_refs: The Back Bay Fens, first link of the Boston park system later called the Emerald Necklace

stops.name: Fairsted, the first office of its kind
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1883 for the move to Brookline; month and day unknown and defaulted. Coordinate corrected to 99 Warren Street, both dossier lenses having pinned it 560 m and 760 m off in different directions
stops.campa: At sixty-one he moves the household out of New York to Brookline, buys an old farmhouse on Warren Street, names it Fairsted, and builds his drafting rooms onto the side of it. It is the first full professional landscape architecture office in the United States: draftsmen, plan files, a photographic record, apprentices who become the next generation, and the two sons who will carry the name. The firm goes on working out of these rooms until 1979, when Congress makes the place a National Historic Site.

The Papers of Frederick Law Olmsted Digital Edition (Rotunda, University of Virginia Press)

stops.name: Franklin Park, composed alone
stops.date_confidence: attested to the later 1880s and 1890s for the construction; 1885 is the dossier's start date, month and day unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: Five hundred acres at the far end of the Boston chain, and this is the last large park he composes by himself: a great open country park of meadow and grazing at one side, a wooded Wilderness of puddingstone ledge and oak at the other, the two held apart so that neither decorates the other. He wants no monuments in it, no flower beds, no attractions of any kind. The money is to go into ground and trees, and the scenery is to be left plain and unpunctuated for people who have come out from the city to be somewhere else for an afternoon.
stops.quote: The idea of the park itself should always be uppermost in the mind of the beholder.
stops.quote_source: Olmsted and Vaux, Description of a Plan for the Improvement of the Central Park (1858; Project Gutenberg #73830)
suggested_refs: Franklin Park, Boston, and Cynthia Zaitzevsky, Frederick Law Olmsted and the Boston Park System (1982)

stops.name: Prospect Point, the falls taken back
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1885 for the creation of the Niagara Reservation; the dossier's two lenses tag the same fact [A] and [R], and it is carried here as reconstruction. 15 July is the opening date of the reservation
stops.campa: For years the American shore of the falls has been fenced, milled, and sold by the peep, with a visitor paying at every gate for a view of moving water. Olmsted, Vaux, and Charles Eliot Norton campaign for the state to buy the shore back and take the mills off it, and in July 1885 the Niagara Reservation opens as free public ground. The two designers then plan its paths and its replanting on a principle Olmsted states plainly: the work of restoration must not itself be visible when it is done.
suggested_refs: The Niagara Reservation, opened 15 July 1885, and the Olmsted-Vaux restoration plan

stops.name: Stanford, the flat riding ground
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the dossier gives 1886 for Leland Stanford's engagement of Olmsted and was not independently re-fetched; month and day unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: Leland Stanford brings him to Palo Alto to plan a university raised as a memorial to a dead son. Olmsted wants the foothills; Stanford wants the flat land where he trained his horses, and Stanford is paying. So Olmsted takes the flat and answers it with a low, close, arcaded quadrangle in a Mediterranean key, courts and colonnades and planting that can live through a rainless summer, arguing that an eastern Georgian college copied onto a California plain would be a lie about the climate. Shepley, Rutan and Coolidge draw the buildings.
suggested_refs: The Main Quadrangle, Stanford University, with Shepley, Rutan and Coolidge

stops.name: Biltmore, the ruined acres made forest
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1888 for the hiring; month and day unknown and defaulted. Coordinate corrected to Biltmore House, the dossier's pin lying 570 m north
stops.campa: George Washington Vanderbilt has bought thousands of worn-out acres near Asheville and wants an English park laid around Richard Morris Hunt's chateau. Olmsted tells him the land will not carry one: the soil is spent, the woods are cut over, and what this ground can honestly be is a working forest managed for timber and for return. Vanderbilt agrees, and the first systematic forestry practised in the United States is carried on across a millionaire's estate because Olmsted talked him out of a lawn. Gifford Pinchot arrives as forester in 1892.
suggested_refs: The Biltmore Forest and Gifford Pinchot's appointment as forester, 1892

stops.name: Jackson Park, the White City
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1890 for the appointment and 1893 for the exposition; month and day unknown and defaulted. Canonical Jackson Park pin inherited unchanged
stops.campa: Chicago wins the exposition and Daniel Burnham calls him in as landscape adviser for a fairground on a raw sand flat beside the lake. He wants the buildings colored and frankly temporary, a pageant that admits it is going to be struck; the architects give him a white classical city instead, and it is the White City the country remembers and copies for forty years. Olmsted's own answer to the sand flat is water: lagoons cut through the site, a wooded island left deliberately quiet in the middle of them, boats as the way people move through the fair.
suggested_refs: The Wooded Island and lagoons, World's Columbian Exposition, Jackson Park, 1893
The Midway Plaisance

stops.name: McLean Hospital, the grounds he did not design
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1898 for the admission and 28 August 1903 for the death; month and day of admission unknown and defaulted. Coordinate corrected to 115 Mill Street, Belmont, both dossier lenses having pinned it 1.1 km and 1.9 km off
stops.campa: His memory has been going since about 1895, the year he withdrew from practice and sat for John Singer Sargent among the rhododendrons at Biltmore. In 1898 his family admits him to McLean Hospital in the Waverley section of Belmont. He had been consulted years earlier on the choice of this site, though the grounds were laid out under the civil engineer Joseph Curtis and no evidence makes the design his, whatever the biographers do with the irony. He lives here five years and dies on the twenty-eighth of August 1903, aged eighty-one.
suggested_refs: John Singer Sargent's 1895 portrait of Olmsted, painted at Biltmore

stops.name: Old North Cemetery, back in Hartford
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1903 for the burial at Old North Cemetery; the day is unknown and defaulted. Three lenses of the dossier gave three different coordinates for this one grave, all roughly 0.9 km off; the mapped position is used
stops.campa: They bring him back to Hartford, a mile from the Main Street store where he was born, and bury him in the Old North Cemetery among the merchants and ministers of the town that sent him away at seven. He is eighty-one. Whether the marker over him is large or plain, nothing reachable now says: the cemetery's own account does not mention his plot, findagrave refuses the page, and the sources that do place the grave disagree with one another by the better part of a mile. Where exactly in the burying ground he lies is an open question.
suggested_refs: Old North Cemetery, Hartford, listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1998
